subjects.name: Telephone
clues: Its inventor suggested that people should answer it by saying 'Ahoy!'
Elisha Gray filed a rival claim for a similar device on the very same day in 1876.
It turns the sound of your voice into electrical signals sent down a wire.
The first words spoken through it were 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
Alexander Graham Bell patented this device for talking over long distances.
subjects.fact: The first telephone exchange opened in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1878.

subjects.name: Light Bulb
clues: Its glowing thread sits inside a glass globe with the air pumped out.
Joseph Swan in England developed one at about the same time as his American rival.
Thomas Edison's team tested thousands of materials for it, later using carbonised bamboo.
When electricity flows through its thin filament, it glows white-hot and brightens a room.
Cartoon characters get one above their heads when they have a bright idea.
subjects.fact: A bulb in a California fire station has been glowing almost non-stop since 1901.

subjects.name: Printing Press
clues: Its design was borrowed from screw machines used to squeeze grapes and olives.
Its metal letters could be rearranged again and again for each new page.
By 1500, millions of books had been made with it across Europe.
It helped Martin Luther's ideas spread quickly across Europe.
Johannes Gutenberg built this machine for making books in Mainz around 1440.
subjects.fact: The Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455, was the first major book made with it in Europe.

subjects.name: Steam Engine
clues: Thomas Newcomen built a working one in 1712 to pump water out of mines.
James Watt made it far more efficient by adding a separate condenser.
It powered factories, ships and locomotives during the Industrial Revolution.
It works by boiling water so that the expanding vapour pushes a piston.
Puffing locomotives like Stephenson's Rocket ran on this kind of power.
subjects.fact: Its power was measured in 'horsepower', a word coined by James Watt.

subjects.name: Phonograph
clues: It recorded sound as dents pressed into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder.
The first words recorded on it came from 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'.
It amazed the public so much that its inventor was nicknamed 'The Wizard of Menlo Park'.
It was the first machine that could both record sound and play it back.
Thomas Edison invented this sound-recording machine in 1877.
subjects.fact: Its inventor later said it was his favourite invention.

subjects.name: Radio
clues: In the 1880s Heinrich Hertz proved that the invisible waves it uses really exist.
In 1901 a signal for it crossed the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
Wireless calls for help using it brought rescue ships to the Titanic in 1912.
Guglielmo Marconi pioneered this way of sending signals without wires in the 1890s.
Stations broadcast music, news and talk shows to it on AM or FM.
subjects.fact: The first regular public broadcasts began in the early 1920s.

subjects.name: Television
clues: Scottish inventor John Logie Baird first showed moving pictures on one in London in 1926.
American Philo Farnsworth built a fully electronic version in 1927.
Early sets showed only black-and-white pictures on small, rounded screens.
Hundreds of millions of people watched the 1969 Moon landing live on one.
This box in the living room shows news, cartoons, sport and soap operas.
subjects.fact: Colour broadcasts became common in the United States in the 1960s.

subjects.name: Dynamite
clues: It was patented in 1867 and made blasting rock far safer than before.
It is made by soaking unstable nitroglycerin into a powdery, absorbent earth.
It helped build tunnels, canals and railways around the world.
The fortune it earned its inventor later paid for famous yearly prizes.
Alfred Nobel invented this explosive, usually sold in paper-wrapped sticks.

links.name: Sweden
links.rel: was invented by an engineer from

subjects.fact: Its name comes from the Greek word 'dynamis', meaning power.

subjects.name: Penicillin
clues: It was first mass-produced during World War II to treat wounded soldiers.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain turned it into a usable drug in Oxford.
It is made by a blue-green mould and kills many kinds of bacteria.
It was the first widely used antibiotic medicine.
Alexander Fleming discovered it in 1928 on a dish of germs in his London lab.
subjects.fact: It has saved many millions of lives since the 1940s.

subjects.name: Paper
clues: Before it, people wrote on clay tablets, silk, bamboo strips and papyrus.
A Han court official, Cai Lun, is credited with improving how it was made in 105 CE.
Early versions were made from tree bark, old rags, hemp and fishing nets.
Its making spread along the Silk Road to the Islamic world and later to Europe.
Books, newspapers and notebooks are printed on sheets of this material.

links.name: Printing Press
links.rel: was made into books by the

subjects.fact: It is one of the 'Four Great Inventions' of ancient China.

subjects.name: Wheel
clues: The oldest known examples date back roughly 5,500 years.
Potters in Mesopotamia used a spinning version to shape clay.
The oldest surviving wooden one, found in a marsh in Slovenia, is over 5,000 years old.
It turns on an axle and makes heavy loads much easier to move.
Often called humanity's greatest invention, it is round and found on every car and bicycle.

links.name: Bicycle
links.rel: is a key part of every

links.name: Automobile
links.rel: is a key part of every

subjects.fact: The potter's version may be even older than the kind used on carts.

subjects.name: Internet
clues: Its ancestor, ARPANET, sent its first message in 1969 and crashed after just 'LO'.
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed its TCP/IP rules in the 1970s.
It switched fully to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983, often called its birthday.
This global network of computers carries email, video calls and websites.
You connect to it through Wi-Fi or mobile data when you go online.
subjects.fact: The first ARPANET message was meant to be 'LOGIN'.

subjects.name: World Wide Web
clues: It was proposed in a March 1989 memo that the author's boss called 'vague but exciting'.
It was born at CERN, the physics laboratory on the French-Swiss border.
Its creator gave it away for free, with no patents or fees.
It joins pages together with hyperlinks that you open in a browser.
Invented by Tim Berners-Lee, it is the system of linked pages you browse online.
subjects.fact: The first website went online in 1991 and explained what the project was.

subjects.name: Microwave Oven
clues: Its inventor, Percy Spencer, worked on radar equipment for the company Raytheon.
He noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted near a radar tube.
The first model, the Radarange, stood almost as tall as a person.
It heats food by making the water molecules inside it jiggle.
This kitchen box warms up leftovers in minutes and makes popcorn pop.
subjects.fact: Spencer's next test after the chocolate bar was popcorn.

subjects.name: iPhone
clues: It was unveiled in January 2007 at the Macworld show in San Francisco.
It was pitched as three devices in one: a music player, a phone and an internet communicator.
Its App Store opened in 2008, a year after the first model went on sale.
Steve Jobs revealed this touchscreen device on stage.
Apple's famous smartphone, released in new generations since 2007.
subjects.fact: The first model went on sale on 29 June 2007.

subjects.name: iPod
clues: It was launched in October 2001 with a 5 GB hard drive.
Its first advertising promised '1,000 songs in your pocket'.
Its famous click wheel let users spin a thumb to scroll through songs.
It synced music using iTunes software, and its ads showed dancing silhouettes.
Apple's pocket music player, sold from 2001 until 2022.

links.name: Walkman
links.rel: followed in the footsteps of the

subjects.fact: Its white earphones became a fashion symbol in the 2000s.

subjects.name: Walkman
clues: It was launched in Japan on 1 July 1979.
Early models had two headphone sockets so two friends could listen together.
Its first version played cassette tapes but could not record music.
It let people carry their music anywhere and listen through light headphones.
Sony's famous portable cassette player.
subjects.fact: Sony co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a way to enjoy music on long flights.

subjects.name: Game Boy
clues: Its design team was led by the engineer Gunpei Yokoi.
Its small screen showed pictures only in shades of greenish grey.
It ran on four AA batteries and fitted in a coat pocket.
In many countries it came packed with the puzzle game Tetris.
Nintendo's famous handheld console from 1989.
subjects.fact: One damaged in the Gulf War still worked and is shown in New York.

subjects.name: PlayStation
clues: It began as a planned CD add-on for a rival company's console before that deal fell apart.
It was launched in Japan in December 1994.
It played games on CDs instead of cartridges.
It became the first home console to sell over 100 million units.
Sony's first home video game console, with circle, cross, square and triangle buttons.
subjects.fact: Its 'father', engineer Ken Kutaragi, had worked on sound chips for Nintendo.

subjects.name: Macintosh
clues: It was introduced in January 1984 with a famous Super Bowl advert.
It came with a mouse and a screen of windows and little picture icons.
Its first model had a built-in 9-inch black-and-white screen.
Its name comes from a variety of apple.
Apple's long-running line of personal computers, launched by Steve Jobs.
subjects.fact: The signatures of its design team were moulded inside the first model's case.

subjects.name: Bicycle
clues: Its 1817 ancestor, built by Karl Drais in Germany, had no pedals at all.
One old version, the penny-farthing, had a giant front wheel.
Its chain-driven 'safety' design from the 1880s is still used today.
The Tour de France is the most famous race for riders of it.
This two-wheeled vehicle is powered by pedalling.

links.name: Wright Brothers
links.rel: was sold and repaired by the

subjects.fact: There are thought to be more than a billion of them in the world.

subjects.name: Airplane
clues: Its first powered flight lasted only 12 seconds.
That historic flight took place near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in December 1903.
Its wings are shaped so that moving air pushes it upwards.
Big jumbo jets of this kind can carry hundreds of passengers.
Invented by the Wright Brothers, it flies people through the sky using wings and engines.
subjects.fact: The 1903 Flyer is displayed at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.

subjects.name: Automobile
clues: Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled petrol-powered version in January 1886.
In 1888 Bertha Benz drove one on the first long-distance road trip.
Henry Ford's moving assembly line made it affordable for ordinary families.
Most run on petrol or diesel, but electric ones are now common.
This four-wheeled road vehicle has a steering wheel, seats and an engine.
subjects.fact: Bertha Benz's trip in 1888 covered about 106 km.

subjects.name: Ford Model T
clues: It was nicknamed the 'Tin Lizzie'.
Buyers could famously have it in 'any colour so long as it is black'.
From 1913 it was built on a moving assembly line.
More than 15 million were built between 1908 and 1927.
The first mass-produced car for ordinary families, made in Michigan by Henry's company.
subjects.fact: Assembly-line production cut the time to build one from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

subjects.name: Volkswagen Beetle
clues: Ferdinand Porsche designed it in the 1930s as a car for ordinary Germans.
Its air-cooled engine sat at the back instead of the front.
Production of the original model finally ended in Mexico in 2003.
Herbie, the film star car with the number 53, was one of these.
This round little car is nicknamed after an insect: the 'Bug'.
subjects.fact: More than 21 million of the original model were built.

subjects.name: Concorde
clues: It first flew in 1969 and was built jointly by Britain and France.
It cruised at about twice the speed of sound.
It could fly from London to New York in about three and a half hours.
Its long nose tilted down to give pilots a better view when landing.
This supersonic passenger airliner was retired in 2003.
subjects.fact: Only 20 were ever built.

subjects.name: Shinkansen
clues: Its first line opened in October 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics.
That first route linked Tokyo and Osaka.
Its long, pointed noses help cut the boom made when entering tunnels.
It is famous for running on time, usually to within seconds.
Japan's world-famous high-speed railway network.
subjects.fact: Its name means 'new trunk line' in Japanese.

subjects.name: Hot Air Balloon
clues: Its first passengers, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
Later in 1783 two men flew one over Paris for about 25 minutes.
The Montgolfier family of paper makers built the first ones.
A burner heats the gas inside its envelope so that it rises.
Passengers ride in a wicker basket beneath this big colourful floating bag.

links.name: Paris
links.rel: made its first crewed flight over

subjects.fact: The 1783 animal flight was watched by King Louis XVI at Versailles.

subjects.name: Apple Inc.
clues: It was founded on 1 April 1976 in California.
Its first product was a hand-built circuit board sold to a local shop.
In 2018 it became the first US company to be valued at one trillion dollars.
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak were among its founders.
This company with a bitten-fruit logo makes the iPhone and the Mac.
subjects.fact: Its first logo showed Isaac Newton sitting under a tree.

subjects.name: Google
clues: It began as a Stanford University research project called BackRub.
Its name plays on a word for the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin set it up in a rented garage in 1998.
It bought YouTube in 2006 and makes the Chrome browser.
Its search engine is so famous that its name became a verb meaning 'search online'.
subjects.fact: Its first ever 'Doodle', in 1998, was a Burning Man festival stick figure.

subjects.name: Microsoft
clues: It was founded in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 1975.
Its name joins the words 'microcomputer' and 'software'.
It supplied the MS-DOS system for IBM's first personal computer in 1981.
It makes the Xbox games console and the Office programs.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded this maker of Windows.
subjects.fact: It moved its headquarters to the Seattle area in 1979.

subjects.name: Tesla, Inc.
clues: It was founded in 2003 by engineers Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning.
Its first vehicle, launched in 2008, was the Roadster sports car.
Elon Musk led its early funding and became its CEO in 2008.
It makes the Model S, Model 3 and Model Y electric cars.
This American electric car maker is named after a famous Serbian-American inventor.
subjects.fact: In 2018 a red Roadster it built was launched into space on a rocket.

subjects.name: Sony
clues: It was founded in Tokyo in 1946 by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita.
One of its early hits was a pocket-sized transistor radio in the 1950s.
It co-developed the compact disc (CD) with Philips.
It created the Walkman portable music player in 1979.
The Japanese electronics giant behind the PlayStation.
subjects.fact: Its name mixes the Latin 'sonus' (sound) with 'sonny', a word for a young boy.

subjects.name: Samsung
clues: It began in 1938 as a small trading company selling dried fish and noodles.
Its name means 'three stars' in Korean.
Part of the group helped build Dubai's record-breaking Burj Khalifa tower.
It makes the Galaxy range of smartphones.
A giant South Korean electronics company.
subjects.fact: It was founded in the city of Daegu.

subjects.name: Nintendo
clues: It began in 1889 in Kyoto, making hand-painted playing cards.
In the 1960s it tried other businesses, including a taxi company and instant rice.
Its 1985 home console, the NES, brought video games back to life in America.
Its Game Boy handheld appeared in 1989.
The Japanese video game company behind Mario and Zelda.
subjects.fact: It still makes traditional hanafuda playing cards.

subjects.name: IBM
clues: It was formed in 1911 by joining companies that made scales, time clocks and punch-card tabulators.
Its nickname is 'Big Blue'.
Its Deep Blue computer beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.
Its Personal Computer of 1981 set the standard for office PCs.
The American computer giant known by three letters, with a striped blue logo.
subjects.fact: It took its current name in 1924.

subjects.name: Lego
clues: It was founded in 1932 by carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen in Billund, Denmark.
Its name comes from Danish words meaning 'play well'.
It made wooden toys before switching to plastic.
Its stud-and-tube interlocking brick was patented in 1958.
This toy brand makes colourful plastic bricks that click together.
subjects.fact: Bricks made in 1958 still fit together with bricks made today.

subjects.name: Nike
clues: It started in 1964 as Blue Ribbon Sports, selling Japanese running shoes.
Co-founder Bill Bowerman made shoe soles using his family's waffle iron.
Its 'Swoosh' logo was designed by a student for just $35.
It is named after the Greek goddess of victory.
This sportswear brand's slogan is 'Just Do It'.
subjects.fact: It is based in Beaverton, Oregon.

subjects.name: Adidas
clues: It is based in Herzogenaurach, a small town in Bavaria.
Its founder's brother started the rival brand Puma in the same town.
Its name comes from its founder, Adolf 'Adi' Dassler.
Its logos feature three stripes.
This German sportswear brand has made the official World Cup football since 1970.

links.name: FIFA World Cup
links.rel: makes the official ball for the

subjects.fact: The rivalry between the two founding brothers split their home town in two.

subjects.name: IKEA
clues: It was founded in 1943 by a 17-year-old in the Swedish countryside.
Its name comes from the founder's initials plus his family farm and village.
It sells flat-pack furniture that customers build themselves.
Its stores famously serve meatballs in their restaurants.
This blue-and-yellow Swedish furniture store sells the Billy bookcase.
subjects.fact: Its product names often come from Swedish places and words.

subjects.name: Toyota
clues: It grew out of a company that made automatic weaving looms.
Its 'just-in-time' way of building things is copied by factories worldwide.
Its Corolla is one of the best-selling cars of all time.
Its Prius, launched in 1997, was the first mass-produced hybrid car.
A Japanese carmaker; its home city was renamed after the company in 1959.
subjects.fact: Its luxury brand is Lexus.

subjects.name: Rolex
clues: It was founded in London in 1905 and later moved to Geneva.
Its Oyster case of 1926 was one of the first waterproof watch cases.
In 1927 swimmer Mercedes Gleitze wore one while swimming the English Channel.
Its logo is a five-pointed golden crown.
This Swiss luxury watch brand makes the Submariner.
subjects.fact: Its founder, Hans Wilsdorf, chose a name that was easy to say in any language.

subjects.name: Levi's
clues: Its founder, a German immigrant, opened a dry goods business in San Francisco in 1853.
In 1873 it patented work trousers strengthened with copper rivets.
Its 501 style is one of the most famous designs in fashion.
Gold miners and cowboys were among its first customers.
This brand is famous for its blue denim jeans.
subjects.fact: The rivet patent was shared with tailor Jacob Davis.

subjects.name: Harley-Davidson
clues: It was founded in 1903 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
Its first motorcycle was built in a small wooden shed.
It was one of only two big American motorcycle makers to survive the Great Depression.
Its machines are known for the deep rumbling sound of their V-twin engines.
This American motorcycle brand is famous for big cruiser bikes and its bar-and-shield logo.
subjects.fact: Its museum opened in Milwaukee in 2008.

subjects.name: YouTube
clues: It was founded in 2005 by three former PayPal employees.
Its first video, 'Me at the zoo', is just 19 seconds long.
Google bought it in 2006 for $1.65 billion.
Creators upload clips to it and can earn money from adverts.
The famous video-sharing website with a red play-button logo.
subjects.fact: Its first video shows co-founder Jawed Karim at San Diego Zoo.

subjects.name: Wikipedia
clues: It was launched on 15 January 2001 by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger.
Its name joins a Hawaiian word meaning 'quick' with the end of 'encyclopedia'.
It is run by a non-profit foundation and paid for by donations.
Anyone can edit its articles, and volunteers check the changes.
The free online encyclopedia with a jigsaw-puzzle globe logo.
subjects.fact: It is written in more than 300 languages.

subjects.name: Facebook
clues: It started in February 2004 in a Harvard University dorm room.
At first, only Harvard students could join.
It added its famous 'Like' button in 2009.
Its parent company renamed itself Meta in 2021.
Mark Zuckerberg's social network.
subjects.fact: It was first called 'TheFacebook'.

subjects.name: eBay
clues: It was started in 1995 by Pierre Omidyar under the name AuctionWeb.
One of the first items sold on it was a broken laser pointer.
It bought PayPal in 2002 and split from it again in 2015.
Buyers bid against each other until a countdown timer runs out.
The famous online auction website.
subjects.fact: The broken laser pointer sold for $14.83 to a collector of broken laser pointers.

subjects.name: Instagram
clues: It launched in October 2010 and was at first only available on the iPhone.
Its early photos were all square, like old instant-camera snapshots.
Facebook bought it in 2012 for about $1 billion.
It is known for photo filters and 24-hour 'Stories'.
The photo- and video-sharing app with a colourful camera logo.
subjects.fact: Its name blends 'instant camera' and 'telegram'.

subjects.name: WhatsApp
clues: It was founded in 2009 by two former Yahoo employees.
Its name is a pun on the greeting 'What's up?'
Facebook bought it in 2014 for about $19 billion.
Two blue ticks show that your message has been read.
This green messaging app sends texts and voice notes over the internet.
subjects.fact: Its founders were Jan Koum and Brian Acton.

subjects.name: TikTok
clues: It is owned by ByteDance, a company based in Beijing.
Its Chinese sister app is called Douyin.
In 2018 it merged with the lip-syncing app Musical.ly.
Its 'For You' page serves up an endless stream of short vertical videos.
This short-video app is famous for dance challenges and viral trends.
subjects.fact: Douyin launched in China in 2016, a year before the international version.

subjects.name: Spotify
clues: It was founded in Stockholm in 2006 by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon.
It opened to the public in 2008.
Its yearly 'Wrapped' feature sums up each user's listening habits.
Its logo shows three curved lines on a green circle.
The Swedish music-streaming app.
subjects.fact: It has a free version supported by adverts and a paid version without them.
